1.rationale: Shelf rails plus a per-card sow line, bold price, and colored stock word make all three facts readable without entering a card; the native month select is simple and predictable. Grouping under late-winter/spring shelves answers season fit structurally.

2.rationale: The product buy box is textbook — price, stock count, quantity input, Add to basket, delivery note — and catalog price/stock sit in conventional card positions. No cleverness anywhere near the money path.

3.rationale: All four traps verified against the data: Black Nebula Carrot reads red 'Out of stock', the null-price Sweet Pea shows 'Price on request', the Chili shows 'Germination 65% (estimated)', and the UK-only banner tops both surfaces plus the buy box. Even 'only 9 packets left' matches stock 9 exactly.

4.rationale: Generous full-width buttons on mobile, native select, and no hover-dependent info suit older tablet readers; the letterspaced small-caps meta lines are the one strain on legibility.

5.rationale: Tokens, serif hierarchy, and packet illustrations carry cleanly across both surfaces and both modes. Minor unevenness inside cards (the Sweet Pea packet face runs taller, shifting its layout) keeps it just short of the top.

6.rationale: Sowing table, difficulty line, potting-shed notes, and companions with price and stock are all on the page with an honest '34 packets' count; a first-time gardener can decide without leaving.

7.rationale: The wooden rack idea is legible in one glance — packet faces, shelf-edge labels, 'the rack by the shop door' copy — and reads as a two-person shop's own furniture, not borrowed gloss.

8.rationale: The only breaks visible are the two declared ones (packet-face cards, shelf rails); price, stock, and basket mechanics keep their exact conventional form.

9.rationale: 'Two of us keep it stocked; every packet is a variety we grow ourselves' and 'From our potting shed' are warm and ownable, though the shelf labels themselves stay mostly functional.

10.rationale: A returning gardener sees season shelves, stock states, and the month filter immediately, and the packet face recurring as the product image ties the two surfaces into one shop.

1.rationale: Price and stock are legible at fixed positions in each numbered entry, but season fit requires reading every meta line — there is no grouping, and the single centered column makes an eight-item scan a long scroll on desktop. The filter itself is simple and predictable.

2.rationale: Buy box, quantity input, stock language, and price placement are all fully conventional; the annual's typography never touches the mechanics.

3.rationale: Out-of-stock is red and honest, the null price becomes 'Price pending — ask us', the estimate is flagged, and 'only 9 packets left' matches the data. The UK-only line is present on both surfaces before any intent, though set small and light.

4.rationale: Body type is comfortable, but the fine letterspaced specimen captions and hairline rules ask more of older eyes than the other systems; targets pass but skew toward text links.

5.rationale: The typographic discipline is exceptional — numbered entries, rules, and consistent rhythm hold across both surfaces and both modes as one printed object.

6.rationale: A conventional buy box sits directly under the title, followed by the year table, potting-shed note, and companions with price and stock — everything a first-timer needs on one quiet page.

7.rationale: The printed seed annual is a form gardeners genuinely trust, and it is executed all the way down to 'No. 1 in the annual' on the product page — provenance love, not boutique gloss.

8.rationale: What I observe matches the declaration exactly: no card chrome anywhere and small-caps specimen captions, with every money mechanic left conventional.

9.rationale: 'Read slowly, choose well' and 'Price pending — ask us' are unhurried, specific, and unmistakably this shop's — no competitor could run them unchanged.

10.rationale: A repeat visitor checking season or stock must scan the whole list or fall back on the filter, since nothing is grouped; the two surfaces do cohere beautifully as one annual.

1.rationale: The deciding question is answered structurally — window groupings, month-band diagrams, bold sow lines, sidebar jump links, and a plain month select — with price and stock at a consistent position in every entry.

2.rationale: The buy box is fully conventional and still lands above the fold on desktop and most tablets despite following the compact year section; stock language and the plain labeled filter are exactly as expected.

3.rationale: All traps check out against the data: red 'Out of stock' carrot, 'Price pending — ask us' for the null price, the estimate flagged twice (inline and in a marginal note), UK-only visible at the top of both surfaces and in the buy box. The month bands match the data windows cell for cell, including the sweet pea's Oct–Nov autumn cells.

4.rationale: The month bands are always backed by bold text ('Sow Feb–Apr'), so no information is graphics-only, and targets are generous; the small italic marginalia are the one concession, but they are supplementary.

5.rationale: Bands, ruled marginalia, and the cream/ink/green/plum palette form one disciplined almanac system across catalog, product page, and both modes.

6.rationale: The year band plus sow/plant/flower table sits directly above an honest buy box, with the margin note and companions closing the loop — a first-time gardener decides on this page.

7.rationale: The almanac-on-the-potting-bench idea reaches every layer — sidebar windows, month bands, grower marginalia — and is service culture, helping the visitor find their month before their packet.

8.rationale: Every unconventional element maps to the two declared breaks (calendar-first organization, almanac marginalia); entry and basket mechanics stay strictly standard.

9.rationale: The knowledgeable neighbor speaks throughout the margins — 'The widest window in the almanac — five months of it', 'for the patient gardener' — warm, specific, and unpublishable by anyone else.

10.rationale: A returning gardener lands on 'find your month first', jumps by window link, and reads stock at a glance; the band recurring on the product page makes the two surfaces one almanac.
